newsitem.title: INDIA: Blasts, protests mark second day of Kashmir voting.
newsitem.headline: Blasts, protests mark second day of Kashmir voting.

text.p: Militants attacked polling stations and protesters mounted a state-wide strike on Monday as India's troubled Jammu and Kashmir state held the second phase of crucial local elections.
Security officials reported at least five blasts, including two grenade attacks, in the separatist stronghold of Anantnag town, 55 km (35 miles) south of the state's summer capital of Srinagar.
Three paramilitary troopers were wounded in one of the grenade attacks, which sent voters scurrying for safety, residents said.

Authorities reported normal to brisk polling in most of the 34 constituencies conducting polls in the second phase of the four-stage elections. Witnesses said turnout in Kashmir was low, but stronger in the state's largely Hindu district of Jammu.

The state, torn by a six-year separatist revolt, is holding its first assembly elections since 1987. The last assembly was dissolved in 1990 after the outbreak of the rebellion in which more than 20,000 people have died.
The polls are considered crucial to India's efforts to restore democratic rule in the region.
The first day of voting in other areas of the state was on September 7, and the last two days will be on September 21 and 30. The results are expected in the first week of October.
Separatist leaders staged demonstrations in several areas of Kashmir including Srinagar, where paramilitary forces used tear gas and wooden batons to disperse the protesters.

At least 20 people, most of them political activists, have been killed during campaigning. Several candidates, including Farooq Abdullah, head of the state's largest party, the National Conference, have escaped attacks.
Some residents in Anatanag as well as neighbouring Pulwama and Bijbehara towns said the army had forced them to vote.

The government denied similar claims during general elections in May and the first stage of assembly polls earlier this month, saying some voters claimed they had been coerced in case of possible retribution by militants.
The government has detained senior leaders of the separatist All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference since last week after they threatened to campaign against the polls, members said.
Separatist groups called a strike on Monday to mark the second round of elections.

"I am voting to bring an end to the rule of bureaucracy," Shakuntala Devi, a Hindu housewife, told Reuters in Jammu. "There is nothing better than having people's own elected representatives to look after our interests."
Jammu and Kashmir is mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state.
"May the Almighty God bring peace to his miserable followers and end their suffering soon," a prayer leader in Srinagar said.
In a bid to quell separatism, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's three-month-old centre-left government has promised to extend "maximum autonomy" to the state following the elections.
On the first day of polling on September 7, voters in 26 of the state's 87 constituencies cast ballots. Officials said between 50 and 53 percent of the eligible voters had turned out that day.
